document_title: UTMB Health adds AI to lung nodule review. About two thirds of its program's nodules came outside screening
_note: Caption carried verbatim from caption.txt. Slide strings polished from storyboard.md and held to the claim quotes in claims.json. Every numeral is in claims.json or figures.json. Drawn to illustrate appears only on S2, S3, S4, S6 and S8. The patient story is attributed to Dr. Nishi on S7 and S8, and S7 never says the AI flagged her nodule. Bunkerhill's 80 percent appears nowhere.
caption:
A scan ordered for something else.

At UTMB Health an AI system reviews lung cancer screening reports and also helps identify nodules found by chance. UTMB says about two thirds of its program's nodules came from patients not having lung cancer screening.

Every flag goes to patient navigator Amanda Rodriguez. A validated risk score helps her decide which follow up comes first.

Medical director Dr. Shawn Nishi calls the AI an assistant, not a decision maker.

Dr. Nishi recalls a patient in her 20s whose scan after a car accident found a nodule. Dr. Nishi says a biopsy showed lung cancer and the patient had surgery intended to cure it. According to Dr. Nishi she had a hereditary disease, and she named seven or eight relatives diagnosed with cancer.

Where you get scanned, who reads the report past the reason it was ordered?

#UTMBHealth #LungCancerScreening #PatientNavigation

S1.headline: The scan was for something else
S1.body: UTMB Health's AI reviews lung cancer screening reports and helps identify nodules found by chance. Each is flagged for a person. UTMB says about two thirds of its program's nodules came from patients not having lung cancer screening.

S2.headline: Weeks, sometimes months
S2.body: UTMB started its lung screening program in 2016. Before the AI, review could take weeks or even months. Medical director Dr. Shawn Nishi says the follow up window had often closed by the time staff reached patients. Folders drawn to illustrate.
strings: UTMB started its lung screening program in 2016. Before the AI, review could take weeks or even months. Medical director Dr. Shawn Nishi says the follow up window had often closed by the time staff reached patients. Folders drawn to illustrate.

S3.headline: Much of the chart review, automated
S3.body: The system was developed with the company Bunkerhill and reviews radiology reports. Chart review was once the slowest part of the work, and much of it is now automated. Pages drawn to illustrate.
strings: Much of the chart review, automated

S4.headline: Every flag goes to a navigator
S4.body: Each nodule is flagged for review by patient navigator Amanda Rodriguez. Her dashboard computes a validated lung cancer risk score so she can decide which follow up comes first. Cards drawn to illustrate.
strings: Every flag goes to a navigator

Each nodule is flagged for review by patient navigator Amanda Rodriguez. Her dashboard computes a validated lung cancer risk score so she can decide which follow up comes first. Cards drawn to illustrate.

S5.headline: It flags. People decide.
S5.body: Dr. Nishi calls the AI an assistant, not a decision maker. The release says people stay at the center while it works in the background.
strings: Dr. Nishi calls the AI an assistant, not a decision maker. The release says people stay at the center while it works in the background.

S6.headline: About 2 in 3 found outside screening
S6.body: About two thirds of the nodules the program found came from patients who were not having lung cancer screening. A nodule counts on any scan that includes part of the lungs. Three lungs drawn to illustrate the share, never a count.
strings: About two thirds of the nodules the program found came from patients who were not having lung cancer screening. A nodule counts on any scan that includes part of the lungs. Three lungs drawn to illustrate the share, never a count.

S7.headline: She was in her 20s
S7.body: Dr. Nishi recalls a patient in her 20s whose scan after a car accident found a nodule nobody was looking for. Dr. Nishi says a biopsy showed lung cancer and she had surgery intended to cure it. Federal screening guidance covers adults aged 50 to 80 who meet its smoking criteria.
strings: Dr. Nishi recalls a patient in her 20s whose scan after a car accident found a nodule nobody was looking for. Dr. Nishi says a biopsy showed lung cancer and she had surgery intended to cure it. Federal screening guidance covers adults aged 50 to 80 who meet its smoking criteria.

S8.headline: Seven or eight relatives
S8.body: Dr. Nishi says the patient named seven or eight relatives who had been diagnosed with cancer. In her account she had a hereditary disease, so her family members needed testing too. Family drawn to illustrate.
strings: Dr. Nishi says the patient named seven or eight relatives who had been diagnosed with cancer. In her account she had a hereditary disease, so her family members needed testing too. Family drawn to illustrate.

S9.headline: At UTMB any scan touching the lungs counts
S9.body: Federal guidance covers screening for adults aged 50 to 80 with a 20 pack-year smoking history who smoke now or quit within the past 15 years. At UTMB a nodule counts on any scan that includes part of the lungs. Ask a doctor what yours showed.
